q: What is a distribution channel?
r: The path a product takes from producer to consumer
Channels can include wholesalers, retailers and online stores.
w: A set of rules for setting prices

q: A manufacturer sells directly to shoppers through its own website. This is an example of a:
r: Direct channel
There are no intermediaries between producer and buyer.
w: A wholesaler would sit between producer and retailer.
A broker would bring buyers and sellers together.

q: Which intermediary buys goods in large quantities and resells them to retailers?
r: Wholesaler
Wholesalers link producers with retailers.
w: Consumers buy for their own use.
A franchisee operates a licensed business.

q: A small candle maker wants its candles in shops across many cities but has no sales staff there. Which decision would help most?
r: Use wholesalers or sales agents to reach retailers
Intermediaries extend reach without building a large sales force.
w: Sell only from the factory door
This limits reach to local visitors.
Cut product quality to lower costs
Lower quality does not solve the reach problem.

q: Which of these is an example of a retailer?
r: A grocery store selling to shoppers
Retailers sell goods to final consumers.
w: A farm selling crops to a processor
This is a producer selling to a business.

q: A company chooses intensive distribution for a candy bar. What does that mean?
r: It sells the candy in as many outlets as possible
Intensive distribution maximizes availability.
w: It sells only through one exclusive store
It sells through a few selected stores
Intensive distribution uses many kinds of outlets.

q: What is market research?
r: Collecting and analyzing information about customers and markets
Research helps businesses make decisions with evidence.
w: Setting the price of a product
This is a retail design task.

q: Which of these is primary data?
r: Survey answers collected directly from customers for the study
Primary data is gathered first-hand for the current purpose.
w: This was collected earlier by someone else.
A magazine article about the industry

q: A cafe wants to know whether local students would buy a new cold brew. Which research method fits best?
r: A short survey of nearby students
A survey asks the target group directly.
w: A review of last year's tax return
Tax records say nothing about student interest.
A study of national coffee exports
Export data does not show local demand.
Drivers do not represent student buyers.

q: A company surveyed only 12 customers before deciding on a nationwide launch. What is the main weakness of this research?
r: The sample is too small to represent all customers
A small sample can give misleading results.
w: Surveys are always too inexpensive to trust
Customers should never be asked questions
Asking customers is a key research method.

q: What is a database of customer purchases most useful for?
r: Spotting buying patterns
Purchase history reveals what customers buy and when.

q: Which of these is secondary data?
r: An industry report published last year
Secondary data was collected earlier for another purpose.
w: Results of a survey you designed
Observations from your own store visits

q: What is a target market?
r: The specific group of customers a business aims to serve
Focusing on a defined group lets the business tailor its offer.

q: Which step comes first when building a marketing plan?
r: Analyzing the current situation
The plan has to be based on facts about the market and the business.
w: Evaluation comes after the plan is carried out.

q: Which tool compares a company's strengths with its competitors'?
r: Competitive analysis
It reveals where a business is ahead or behind.
w: This shows when sales cover costs.

q: A bike shop sets the objective to raise e-bike sales by 15 percent in 12 months. What must the plan add to be complete?
r: Strategies and actions to reach the objective
An objective needs a plan for how it will be achieved.
w: A logo does not explain how to reach the goal.
This does not address the objective.

q: What does market share measure?
r: A company's percentage of total sales in a market
It shows how large a business is compared with its rivals.
w: Market share is about sales share, not profit.

q: A company learns that most of its buyers are aged 18 to 24. How should this shape the plan?
r: Aim promotion at that age group
Data about buyers should guide targeting.
w: The data does not point to a price change.

q: A store adds a 40 percent markup to the $50 cost of a jacket. What is the selling price?
r: A 40 percent markup on $50 is $20, so the price is $70.
w: This adds 40 dollars instead of 40 percent.
This is the markup amount only.
This treats the markup as 10 percent.

q: A new company launches with a very low price to win customers quickly. Which strategy is this?
r: Penetration pricing
Low entry prices help a product gain market share fast.
w: Prestige pricing sets high prices to signal quality.
This sets price by adding a markup to cost.

q: Which factor most directly sets the minimum price a business can charge without losing money?
r: Its total cost per unit
A price below cost produces a loss on each sale.
w: Colors do not set a price floor.
Hours do not set a price floor.
A slogan does not set a price floor.

q: A retailer cuts an item's price from $80 to $60. By what percent was it marked down?
r: 25 percent
The $20 drop is 25 percent of $80.
w: This treats the dollar drop as a percent.
This uses the new price as the base.
This confuses the new price with the discount.

q: What is price skimming?
r: Setting a high introductory price and lowering it over time
Skimming captures early buyers willing to pay more.
w: Always charging the lowest price in the market
Matching a competitor's price every week

q: Pricing an item at $4.99 instead of $5.00 is an example of:
r: Psychological pricing
Prices just under a round number seem lower to buyers.
w: This groups products at one price.
This sells below cost to attract traffic.

q: What is a product line?
r: A group of related products sold by one company
A line shares a brand or purpose.
w: The route of a delivery truck

q: In which stage of the product life cycle are sales low and promotion costs high?
r: Introduction
New products need heavy promotion to build awareness.

q: A company adds a new flavor to an existing snack brand. What is this called?
r: Product line extension
Adding a variation widens the existing line.
w: This is a dispute among channel members.
This is a product becoming outdated.

q: Sales of a mature product are flat while competition grows. Which action is most likely to extend its life?
r: Update its features or find new uses and markets
Fresh features or new customers can restart growth.
w: Less promotion is unlikely to help.
This ends the product instead of extending it.
Raise the price without any change
A higher price alone is unlikely to improve sales.

q: Besides protecting a product, what is another main purpose of packaging?
r: Promoting and identifying the product
Packaging carries the brand and helps shoppers recognize it.

q: What is a warranty mainly intended to do?
r: Give buyers confidence the product will work as promised
A warranty backs the seller's promise about quality.
w: Limit how many units can be sold
Warranties do not control sales volume.
The purpose is assurance, not cost.

q: Which of these is an element of the promotional mix?
r: Advertising
Advertising, sales promotion, public relations and personal selling make up the mix.

q: A store gives out free samples of a new snack. This is an example of:
r: Sales promotion
Samples are short-term incentives to try a product.
w: This is a seller talking one-on-one to persuade a buyer.
This sends printed messages to addresses.

q: A new brand's ad explains what the product is and how it works. This ad is mainly:
r: Informative
Informative ads explain features and uses.
w: Reminder ads keep a known brand in mind.
Institutional ads promote a company's image.

q: A company wants to reach teenagers on a limited budget. Which approach is most cost-effective?
r: Social media posts and partnerships aimed at teens
These reach the target group at low cost.
w: A national TV ad during the evening news
This is expensive and not aimed at teens.
A full-page ad in a business journal
The readers are not the target.
A billboard in a distant city
It is unlikely to reach the target group.

q: What is public relations?
r: Building goodwill through communication with the public and press
PR shapes how the public views a company.

q: A loyalty program gives a free coffee after 10 purchases. What does it mainly aim to do?
r: Encourage repeat purchases
Rewards give customers a reason to come back.
w: This is a side effect, not an aim.

q: What is the first step in the selling process?
r: Prospecting
Finding potential customers comes before approaching them.
w: Objections come up during the presentation.

q: A customer says, 'It's too expensive.' Which response best handles this objection?
r: Acknowledge the concern and explain the product's value
This respects the customer and shows what they get for the price.
w: Argue that the customer is wrong
Raise the price to seem exclusive

q: Which question is an open-ended question a salesperson might ask?
r: What features matter most to you?
Open-ended questions invite longer answers.
w: This can be answered yes or no.
Are you ready to buy today?

q: After selling a phone, a salesperson suggests a case and a screen protector. This technique is called:
r: Suggestive selling
Suggestive selling recommends add-ons related to the purchase.
w: This contacts people with no prior relationship.
This meets a competitor's lower price.
This is finding new potential customers.

q: Why do salespeople follow up with customers after the sale?
r: To make sure customers are satisfied and encourage repeat business
Follow-up builds relationships.
w: Prices are not changed after the sale.
Follow-up is meant to keep in touch.
This is not a purpose of follow-up.

q: A salesperson who lists a product's features and then explains how each helps the customer is using:
r: Feature-benefit selling
Linking features to benefits shows what the product does for the buyer.
w: This is a way of finding prospects.
This simply records what customers ask for.
